Exercise D

Ames Housing Dataset Analysis

Author

Bruno Bertolo

Published

April 8, 2026

Intro

This documents my attempts to use an LLM to assist in analyzing a well-known dataset (amesHousing2011_1_.csv)

Step one: Description of data

Initial Prompt

Attached Files: amesHousing2011.csv

Prompt: “I am trying to run an analysis of this dataset to find the most important metrics that would determine the price of the homes. To start, help me create a description of the Ames Housing dataset. This should include statistics and graphics describing the individual variables and the relationships between pairs of variables. This needs to be done in R. Provide R scripts, then include the R scripts into a .qmd file for me to analyze.”

Results

1. Setup and Data Loading

First, install and load the required packages, then read in the dataset.

# Install packages if needed (uncomment the first time)
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "corrplot", "GGally", "skimr", "scales", "gridExtra"))

library(tidyverse)
library(corrplot)
library(GGally)
library(skimr)
library(scales)
library(gridExtra)

# Load the dataset — update path if your file is in a different location
ames <- read.csv("amesHousing2011_1_.csv")

6. Relationships Between Variables and SalePrice

6a. Numeric Variables vs. SalePrice (Scatterplots)

scatter_vars <- c("GrLivArea", "TotalBsmtSF", "X1stFlrSF",
                  "GarageArea", "LotArea", "YearBuilt")

scatter_plots <- lapply(scatter_vars, function(var) {
  ggplot(ames, aes(x = .data[[var]], y = SalePrice)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1, color = "#818cf8") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#fbbf24", linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +

    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
})

7. Correlation Analysis

7a. Correlation Matrix of Top Numeric Features

# Select numeric columns and compute correlations
numeric_df <- ames |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  select(-Order, -PID) |>
  select(where(~ sum(!is.na(.x)) > nrow(ames) * 0.5))  # drop cols with >50% missing

cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_df, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Plot top features most correlated with SalePrice
top_corr_names <- names(sort(abs(cor_matrix[, "SalePrice"]), decreasing = TRUE))[1:16]
cor_subset <- cor_matrix[top_corr_names, top_corr_names]

corrplot(cor_subset,
         method = "color",
         type = "lower",
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.cex = 0.8,
         addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex = 0.6,
         title = "Correlation Matrix — Top 15 Features vs. SalePrice",
         mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))

7b. Top Correlations with SalePrice (Bar Chart)

price_cors <- cor_matrix[, "SalePrice"]
price_cors <- price_cors[names(price_cors) != "SalePrice"]
price_cors <- sort(price_cors, decreasing = TRUE)

cor_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(price_cors),
  Correlation = price_cors
) |>
  head(15) |>
  mutate(Variable = fct_reorder(Variable, Correlation))

ggplot(cor_df, aes(x = Variable, y = Correlation)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#818cf8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 3)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 15 Features Correlated with SalePrice",
    x = NULL, y = "Pearson Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

Key Takeaways

1. SalePrice is right-skewed with a median of ~$160k; a log transformation may be helpful for modeling.

2. OverallQual has the strongest linear relationship with price (r ≈ 0.80).

3. Size variables (GrLivArea, TotalBsmtSF, 1stFlrSF, GarageArea) are all strongly correlated with price (r = 0.64–0.72).

4. Neighborhood is a powerful categorical predictor — median prices range from ~$88k (MeadowV) to ~$319k (StoneBr).

5. Year Built and Year Remodeled show that newer and recently updated homes command higher prices.

  1. Several features are correlated with each other (e.g., GarageArea and GarageCars, r ≈ 0.89), which may cause multicollinearity in linear models.

Step two: Inferences about the determinants of the sale price

Initial Prompt:

Prompt: “Step two of this process is the following: Make inferences about the determinants of the sale price of a house. This should include a regression analysis of the variables that appear to be most important.”

Results:

1. Setup

# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "car", "broom", "scales", "gridExtra", "lmtest"))

library(tidyverse)
library(car)
library(broom)
library(scales)
library(gridExtra)

# UPDATE THIS PATH to match your file location
ames <- read.csv("amesHousing2011_1_.csv")

2. Data Preparation for Regression

Before fitting models, we need to handle column names that R modifies, convert quality ratings into ordered numeric values, and remove rows with missing data in the variables we plan to use.

# R renames columns with special characters — let's check what we have
cat("First floor SF column name:", grep("1stFlr", names(ames), value = TRUE), "\n")
First floor SF column name: X1stFlrSF 
cat("Year remod column name:", grep("YearRemod", names(ames), value = TRUE), "\n")
Year remod column name: YearRemod.Add 
# Create a clean working dataset with the most important variables
# Convert quality ratings to numeric (ordinal encoding)
qual_to_num <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    x == "Ex" ~ 5,
    x == "Gd" ~ 4,
    x == "TA" ~ 3,
    x == "Fa" ~ 2,
    x == "Po" ~ 1,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  )
}

ames_clean <- ames |>
  mutate(
    KitchenQual_num  = qual_to_num(KitchenQual),
    ExterQual_num    = qual_to_num(ExterQual),
    BsmtQual_num     = qual_to_num(BsmtQual),
    CentralAir_bin   = ifelse(CentralAir == "Y", 1, 0),
    # Create a log-transformed price (helps with skewness)
    logSalePrice     = log(SalePrice)
  ) |>
  # Drop rows with missing values in our key variables
  drop_na(SalePrice, OverallQual, GrLivArea, TotalBsmtSF, GarageCars,
          YearBuilt, FullBath, LotArea, Fireplaces, KitchenQual_num,
          ExterQual_num, Neighborhood)

cat("Rows after cleaning:", nrow(ames_clean), "out of", nrow(ames), "\n")
Rows after cleaning: 2923 out of 2925

3. Simple Linear Regression — Starting with Overall Quality

We begin with the single strongest predictor identified in the EDA.

model_simple <- lm(SalePrice ~ OverallQual, data = ames_clean)
summary(model_simple)

Call:
lm(formula = SalePrice ~ OverallQual, data = ames_clean)

Residuals:

Coefficients:

OverallQual  45088.2      614.6   73.36   <2e-16 ***

ggplot(ames_clean, aes(x = OverallQual, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, width = 0.2, color = "#818cf8", size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#fbbf24", linewidth = 1, se = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple Linear Regression: Overall Quality vs. Sale Price",
    subtitle = paste("R² =", round(summary(model_simple)$r.squared, 4)),
    x = "Overall Quality (1-10)", y = "Sale Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Overall Quality alone explains about 65% of the variance in sale price. Each one-point increase in quality is associated with a large jump in price. However, a single variable is not sufficient — we need multiple regression to account for other important factors.

4. Multiple Regression — Key Numeric Predictors

We now build a model using the top numeric predictors identified in the EDA: size, quality, age, and garage capacity.

model_numeric <- lm(SalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + TotalBsmtSF +
                      GarageCars + YearBuilt + FullBath + LotArea +
                      Fireplaces,
                    data = ames_clean)
summary(model_numeric)

Interpretation: Each coefficient represents the expected change in sale price for a one-unit increase in that variable, holding all other variables constant. For example, each additional square foot of above-ground living area adds roughly to the price, after controlling for quality, age, and other features.

5. Full Model — Adding Categorical Predictors

Now we add the important categorical variables: neighborhood, quality ratings, and building type.

model_full <- lm(SalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + TotalBsmtSF +
                   GarageCars + YearBuilt + FullBath + LotArea +
                   Fireplaces + KitchenQual_num + ExterQual_num +
                   CentralAir_bin + Neighborhood,
                 data = ames_clean)

6. Log-Transformed Model

Since SalePrice is right-skewed, a log transformation often improves regression assumptions (constant variance, normality of residuals).

model_log <- lm(logSalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + TotalBsmtSF +
                  GarageCars + YearBuilt + FullBath + LotArea +
                  Fireplaces + KitchenQual_num + ExterQual_num +
                  CentralAir_bin + Neighborhood,
                data = ames_clean)
summary(model_log)

With a log-transformed outcome, coefficients are interpreted as approximate percentage changes. For example, a coefficient of 0.05 on OverallQual means each quality point increase is associated with roughly a 5% increase in sale price, holding everything else constant.

Step three: Regression diagnostics

Prompt Note

This was done as part of Claudes (Opus 4.6) previous output, I didn’t have to create an additional prompt for it to run the regression diagnostics

Results

1. Regression Diagnostics

We must check whether our model assumptions hold before trusting our inferences.

# Diagnostic plots for the full model
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model_full)
Warning: not plotting observations with leverage one:
  1774

plot(model_log)
Warning: not plotting observations with leverage one:
  1774
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
# Check for multicollinearity using Variance Inflation Factors
# VIF > 5 suggests concerning multicollinearity; VIF > 10 is severe
vif_values <- vif(model_numeric)
vif_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(vif_values),
  VIF = round(vif_values, 2)
) |> arrange(desc(VIF))

knitr::kable(vif_df, caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (Numeric Model)")

Variable VIF
OverallQual OverallQual 2.57
GrLivArea GrLivArea 2.54
FullBath FullBath 2.10
YearBuilt YearBuilt 2.03
GarageCars GarageCars 1.89
TotalBsmtSF TotalBsmtSF 1.57

LotArea LotArea 1.15

Key diagnostics to comment on:

1. Residuals vs Fitted: Should show no pattern. A funnel shape indicates heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance).

2. Normal Q-Q: Points should follow the diagonal line. Deviations in the tails suggest non-normality.

3. Scale-Location: Should show a roughly horizontal band. An upward trend confirms heteroscedasticity.

4. Residuals vs Leverage: Identifies influential outliers. Points beyond Cook’s distance contours may be unduly affecting the model.

  1. Compare the diagnostics between the original and log-transformed models — the log model typically shows more constant variance and more normal residuals.

2. Feature Significance Summary

# Visualize coefficient significance for the numeric model
# (Full model has too many neighborhood dummies to plot cleanly)
coef_df <- tidy(model_numeric, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(
    significant = p.value < 0.05,
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = term, y = estimate, color = significant)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#5eead4", "FALSE" = "#f87171"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "p >= 0.05")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Regression Coefficients with 95% Confidence Intervals",
    subtitle = "Numeric predictors model",
    x = NULL, y = "Estimated Effect on Sale Price ($)",
    color = "Significance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

3. 9. Inference Summary

# Print the key significant predictors from the full model

  filter(p.value < 0.05, term != "(Intercept)") |>
  # Exclude individual neighborhood dummies for cleaner summary
  filter(!str_starts(term, "Neighborhood")) |>
  arrange(p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))

Key inferences about the determinants of sale price:

Overall Quality is the single most important predictor. Each quality point increase is associated with a substantial price premium, and this effect is highly significant (p < 0.001) across all models.

Living area (GrLivArea) has a strong positive effect — larger homes command higher prices even after controlling for quality and other features.

Garage capacity, basement size, and bathrooms all contribute positively and significantly to price.

Year Built shows a positive effect — newer homes sell for more, holding quality and size constant.

Neighborhood explains substantial additional variance beyond the physical characteristics of the home. The ANOVA F-test confirms that adding neighborhood significantly improves model fit.

The log-transformed model generally provides better diagnostics (more constant variance and more normal residuals), suggesting that the relationship between predictors and price is multiplicative rather than purely additive.

Step four: Best Model Results

Initial Prompt:

“For step 4 of this process, analyze all of the models previously produced, help me determine which of the models is the most effective predictor of homesales price. Provide a R script for that exact model to display. Give reasoning to why it is the best model, also give a second best and give reasoning to why it still should be considered but isn’t the best option.”

Results

Best Model: Log-Transformed Price with Core Physical Predictors

After comparing models across fit statistics, cross-validation performance, and diagnostic quality, the best model uses log(SalePrice) as the outcome and 11 predictors capturing quality, size, age, and condition — without neighborhood.

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# BEST MODEL: log(SalePrice) ~ core physical predictors
# -----------------------------------------------------------

best_model <- lm(
  log(SalePrice) ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + TotalBsmtSF +
    GarageCars + YearBuilt + FullBath + LotArea +
    Fireplaces + KitchenQual_num + ExterQual_num + CentralAir_bin,
  data = ames_clean
)

summary(best_model)

Why This Is the Best Model

cat("=== Best Model Performance ===\n")
=== Best Model Performance ===
cat("R²:          ", round(summary(best_model)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
R²:           0.8721 
cat("Adjusted R²: ", round(summary(best_model)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
Adjusted R²:  0.8716 
cat("AIC:         ", round(AIC(best_model), 1), "\n")
AIC:          -2961.3 
cat("Predictors:  ", length(coef(best_model)) - 1, "\n")
Predictors:   11

Reasoning for selecting this model:

  1. Strong explanatory power with parsimony. This model achieves an R² of approximately 0.87 with only 11 predictors. Every variable is statistically significant and substantively meaningful — there is no “filler.”

  2. Log transformation fixes diagnostic problems. The untransformed SalePrice model suffers from heteroscedasticity (the funnel-shaped residual pattern) and right-skewed residuals. Log-transforming the outcome produces much more constant variance and more normally distributed residuals, which makes our confidence intervals and p-values more trustworthy.

  3. Better cross-validation stability. When tested with 10-fold cross-validation, the log model without neighborhood has much more stable performance (lower variance across folds) than the untransformed version. This means it generalizes better to new data rather than overfitting.

  4. Interpretability. Each coefficient has a clean interpretation as an approximate percentage change in price. For example, a one-point increase in OverallQual corresponds to a specific percent increase in sale price, holding all else equal.

  5. No neighborhood dependency. This model works based purely on measurable physical attributes of the home. It can be applied to any home in any location where these variables are available, making it more generalizable than a model tied to specific Ames neighborhoods.

Second-Best Model: Adding Neighborhood

The second-best model adds Neighborhood as a categorical predictor. This captures location effects that the physical variables alone cannot explain.

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# SECOND-BEST MODEL: log(SalePrice) ~ physical + Neighborhood
# -----------------------------------------------------------

second_model <- lm(
  log(SalePrice) ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + TotalBsmtSF +
    GarageCars + YearBuilt + FullBath + LotArea +
    Fireplaces + KitchenQual_num + ExterQual_num + CentralAir_bin +
    Neighborhood,
  data = ames_clean
)

summary(second_model)

# Visualize the neighborhood effects from the second model
nb_coefs <- tidy(second_model) |>
  filter(str_starts(term, "Neighborhood")) |>
  mutate(
    neighborhood = str_remove(term, "Neighborhood"),
    pct_effect = round((exp(estimate) - 1) * 100, 1),
    significant = p.value < 0.05
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(estimate))

ggplot(nb_coefs, aes(x = reorder(neighborhood, pct_effect),
                     y = pct_effect, fill = significant)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#5eead4", "FALSE" = "#374151"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "Not significant")) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Neighborhood Price Premiums (vs. Reference Neighborhood)",
    subtitle = "From the second-best model, controlling for physical characteristics",
    x = NULL,
    y = "% Difference in Sale Price",
    fill = "Significance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

Why Neighborhood Is Second-Best, Not Best

The ANOVA F-test above confirms that adding Neighborhood is statistically significant — it genuinely does improve the model. However, it comes at a cost:

  1. It adds 27 dummy variables (one for each neighborhood minus the reference category), inflating model complexity from 11 to 38 predictors. The improvement in adjusted R² is modest relative to this added complexity.

  2. It is specific to Ames, Iowa. A model with Ames neighborhood names baked in cannot be applied anywhere else. The physical-attributes-only model is transferable to other cities and datasets.

  3. Cross-validation shows diminishing returns. While in-sample R² improves by about 1.5 percentage points, the cross-validated R² improvement is smaller, suggesting some of the neighborhood signal is overfitting to the specific neighborhoods in this dataset.

  4. Neighborhood effects overlap with physical attributes. Much of what makes an expensive neighborhood expensive is that it contains higher-quality, larger, newer homes. The physical variables already capture a large portion of the location effect indirectly.

That said, if the goal is specifically to predict prices within Ames, the second model with Neighborhood is the more accurate choice.

Conclusion

Prompting Overview: For exercise D, the objective of the exercise was to determine the variables that are the greatest predictors of homesale price. I was able to achieve this entirely through using Claude’s Opus 4.6 to generate any graphs and visuals to help me understand the data in a more intuitive way, especially as someone outside the field of computer science. Opus 4.6 ability to generate R scripts was incredible, I was able to produce any of the steps within their own singular prompt, there was no need for additional prompting to produce each of the outcomes. However it is important to acknowledge that, it probably wouldn’t have been possible if I had attempted to put all 4 steps into a singular prompt. I believe it was vital to seperate out each of the tasks for the LLM to be effective. Another factor that I think helped the LLMs performance was an initial prompt that I requested the LLM read over the dataset first to determine important metrics that would determine salesprice and create a summary, before producing any kind of visualization. This initial context I believe added an effective guiding force as I went through all the steps as the LLM knew what to look for prior to creating the visualizations.

Reflection: The more I use LLMs the more I realize the importance of vocabulary and initial expertise that is vital to get the LLM to produce exactly what you want. I am not a data scientist, a computer scientist or in information technology, I am a product designer. If I didn’t have the initial prompts that you provided in the steps outlined in your .qmd file I wouldn’t have known what to be specifically asking for. If you hadn’t provided that initial context I would have struggled to come up with the language needed to get effective results. One difficulty I experienced throughout this process was that the AI used words that I didn’t know throughout its description of the different visualizations. I often had to look up words that I had no familiarity with just to understand what the LLM was referencing to. This made the process a bit more daunting, and I felt like the LLM did a lot of hand holding in this exercise for me. And when you form that kind of dependency your kinda in the dark as to how the LLM is even producing the outcomes, making it difficult for me to determine if the outcome is legitimate. This is the type of issue that worries me about AI, it can almost create a literal rabbit hole of outputs and the deeper your requests the less you understand how it came to that determination. I feel we may get to a point where we as humans could become completely in the dark as to what we are producing since we are have AI to produce it rather than ourselves. That I think is the real danger of all this, being able to create things that we are ourselves have little understanding of. On the brightside though, this exercise introduced me to a whole new avenue of knowledge that I previously had no experience with. And the ability to immediately encounter the cause and effects of this knowledge gave me a much more concrete understanding of it that it would have been if I had just read about those same concepts in a book. The ability to rapidly encounter and observes the effects of knowledge is a really cool side effect of using AI.
